question_type: Absolute difference of one expenditure category between two fiscal years that no single issue prints together, with the series defined by a footnote paraphrase

opus_path.decision: Took the quantity to be federal 'Public works' general expenditures for fiscal years 1934 and 1946, in $M. Treated the qualifier as a series selector: the column whose footnote includes the Public Works Administration and housing (USHA/FPHA) and excludes FWA war-activity public works from July 1941. Noted up front that no single issue holds both years.
An FTS search on the footnote wording led to Table 3 'Analysis of General Expenditures'. The same footnote appears from 1941_10 through 1948_02.

Ran a systematic per-vintage scan (scan_pw.py) of every 1939-1949 issue for public-works cells in the 1934 and 1946 rows and grouped the values by definition. It rejected: pre-1941_10 FY1934 printings (footnote has no housing or war exclusion); 1939-40 narrower sub-series; and 1948_03+ FY1946 printings (housing moved to its own column). It chose FY1934 from 1941_10..1944_06 and FY1946 from 1946_08..1948_01.

Found and rejected OCR hazards: 1944_04's FY1934 cell fails the row sum; the 1946_05 rows labelled 1930-1934 are really FY1936-1940; 1946_09 has a column shift; 1947_04's FY1946 row is split by a footnote-marker cell; 1948_02's FY1946 cell is garbled.
FY1934 from the 1944_06 Table 3 'Public Works 2/ 3/' column; FY1946 from the 1947_11 Table 3 'Other general expenditures > Public works 1/' column. Each value is identical across its vintage range.
Row-sum cross-checks on both rows, plus the 1946_08 budget-summary 'Public works' line for FY1946.

Saw the 1945_09+ 'general expenditures now include revolving funds; back figures revised' rebasing. Chose NOT to harmonize, because no issue publishes FY1934 on that basis and both printed cells carry the footnote definition the question paraphrases.
Absolute difference of the two printed cells, done in calc.py.

opus_key_moves: Mapped the question's qualifier to a specific footnote and used that footnote as the series identity across two vintages.
Scanned every vintage exhaustively and used row-sum checks to reject OCR-mislabelled, split or shifted rows (1946_05 year labels, 1947_04 split cell, 1944_04/1948_02 garbles).
Refused to build an unpublished rebased value; used only printed cells that share the definition.

first_divergence.what_glm_did: Read the FY1946 row of 1947_04 Table 3, where an OCR-split footnote marker ('11/') occupies its own cell and shifts every later cell one column right. It mapped cells to headers by position and took the Social Security program value as Public works.
first_divergence.what_opus_did: Took FY1946 from 1947_11:292, where the marker is merged into the agriculture cell. It flagged the 1947_04 split and the 1946_09 shift and confirmed the cell with row sums and the 1946_08 summary line.
first_divergence.why_glm_went_that_way: [46] states the value with no mapping shown. At [66] it explicitly aligned the 1946_12 row by treating the 'agriculture value + footnote' cell as the Social Security cell, so it did try to align but anchored on the wrong column. It never ran a sum check.
first_divergence.consequence: The FY1946 endpoint came from the neighbouring column. Together with the FY1934 misread, the final difference is roughly 3x Opus's.

secondary_errors.note: Picked a correct vintage and table for FY1934 (1942_08 Table 3, with the matching PWA/housing/war-exclusion footnote), but took the Aid-to-agriculture cell, one column right of Public Works, in a cleanly aligned row.

Saw a FY1946 Public works value in the 1947_02 budget summary that agrees with Opus's cell. It dismissed it as 'budget document classification' instead of treating the disagreement with its own 1947_04 read as a red flag.

saw_correct_evidence.where: [53] output shows the 1942_08 FY1934 row with the correct Public Works cell; [32]/[56] a FY1946 value matching Opus's; [65] the 1946_12 FY1946 row, which contains the correct cell.

glm_expressed_doubt.where: [56] 'let's not rush' (about the FY1934 vintage, not the column mapping); [66] noticed 'columns shifted due OCR' but resolved the shift the wrong way.

remedies.intervention: Row extractor that returns {header: cell} for a named row, merges stray footnote-marker tokens ('11/', '13/') into the preceding cell, and warns when the row's cell count differs from the header count.
remedies.why: Both of this arm's errors are positional column misreads, and one is in a cleanly aligned row. A named-cell tool removes the counting step entirely.

remedies.intervention: Cross-printing and components-sum check on every extracted cell: re-read the same (row, column) in two or more other printings and block the commit on disagreement.
remedies.why: FY1934 is printed identically in many 1941_10-1944_06 issues and FY1946 in 1946_08-1948_01. The arm itself saw a disagreeing FY1946 value at [56] and ignored it.

remedies.intervention: Match columns by header name, never by position. OCR footnote markers (NN/) can occupy their own cell and shift the rest of the row.
remedies.why: The prompt arm, whose context had a 'match columns by header, never by position' convention, read these same cells correctly [36].

first_divergence.what_glm_did: Had Opus's exact two cells and difference at [36] (FY1934 from the 1944 Table 3, FY1946 from the 1947_01 Table 3) and confirmed both were stable across printings [43]-[46]. It then read 'revised WWII-era figures' as the 1945_09+ rebasing that folds in revolving funds. It showed that the rebased FY1937-1940 cells equal the old Public Works cell plus the Table 5 revolving-fund public-works cell, and built a rebased FY1934 the same way: a number printed nowhere, as its own searches [49] and [51] confirmed.
first_divergence.what_opus_did: Noticed the same rebasing but rejected harmonizing: no issue publishes FY1934 on that basis, and both printed cells carry the footnote definition the question paraphrases.
first_divergence.why_glm_went_that_way: [46]-[48]: mixing the older FY1934 basis with the rebased FY1946 basis looked 'inconsistent', and it took 'Use revised WWII-era figures' as an instruction to avoid that. [58] 'So reconstruct.'
first_divergence.consequence: The FY1934 endpoint was inflated by the added revolving-fund component, so the committed difference is roughly 2x Opus's.

saw_correct_evidence.where: [36] explicitly computed the same two cells and difference as Opus and called it 'plausible'; [43]-[46] verified both cells were stable across printings.

glm_expressed_doubt.where: [48] 'Need determine builder likely expects...'; [60] conceded that 'revised WWII-era figures' 'could simply mean use 1944/1947 tables rather than 1939 unrevised' and then kept the reconstruction.

adapter_context.relevant_item: L-commit-once ('After any computation that produces a candidate number, commit the bare value FIRST; further searching is justified only by a specific, named discrepancy'); Conventions 'Vintage by row type: ANNUAL rows take the latest final vintage'; Procedure step 1 (compare with the latest bulletin carrying the row)
adapter_context.notes: No L-id is cited in any THINK. Commit-once would have locked in the correct candidate at [36]. The repeated 'use the latest revision' guidance fits its rationale that the revised basis must govern both endpoints. The learner later added L-public-works-column-pwa-housing ('never add the revolving-funds cell'), which is question-specific.

remedies.intervention: Provenance gate: every input to the final computation must be a cited file:line cell that exists verbatim in the corpus. A derived or adjusted input blocks the commit until the actor either reverts to printed cells or states why no published value exists.
remedies.why: The synthesized FY1934 input was searched for and not found ([49], [51]) and the actor went ahead anyway. A gate would have returned it to the published-cell answer it had at [36].

remedies.intervention: Commit-first-then-challenge: once a candidate exists, record it as the incumbent. A later alternative replaces it only if a reviewer pass accepts a named test (e.g. 'is the adjusted input published anywhere?').
remedies.why: L-commit-once existed as text in this context and was not followed. A control-flow incumbent does not depend on the actor remembering the lesson.

remedies.intervention: Do not harmonize bases across vintages by constructing unpublished values. When the question paraphrases a footnote definition, use the printed cells whose footnote matches, even if a later rebasing exists.
remedies.why: Addresses the exact rationale at [48]. The learner judged text sufficient (it added such a lesson later), but this arm ignored adjacent text such as commit-once.

first_divergence.what_glm_did: Applied card C003's 'take each endpoint ... from the latest issue printing that fiscal year', a card scoped to agency outlays ([36]: 'It says department outlays but general principle'). It took FY1934 from 1946_05, the latest file with a row labelled 1934. That '1934' row is an OCR year-mislabel of FY1940: 1946_05's rows labelled 1930-1934 are really FY1936-1940.
first_divergence.what_opus_did: Scanned all vintages, identified the 1946_05 mislabel (its values equal the FY1936-1940 rows of 1946_07/08), and took FY1934 from the 1941_10..1944_06 printings (1944_06:1201).
first_divergence.why_glm_went_that_way: Explicit card citation at [36]. The [29] file list showed about 45 issues with both 1934 and 1946 rows in this table, and it picked the latest instead of comparing printings.
first_divergence.consequence: The FY1934 endpoint is really a FY1940 value. FY1946 was read correctly at [47], and the committed difference is almost 4x Opus's.

secondary_errors.note: Noticed that 1947_02's row labelled 1940 carries exactly the values of 1946_05's '1934' row ('OCR mislabels?') but explained it away. It never compared against the earlier FY1934 printings in its own [29] list, whose totals differ.

saw_correct_evidence.where: [29] listed the 1941_10..1944_06 files that carry the correct FY1934 row but never opened them; [51] saw the duplicate-values evidence of the mislabel; FY1946 correct at [47].

glm_expressed_doubt.where: [51] 'OCR mislabels?' ... then 'Could be duplicate due OCR?' before settling on the mislabelled row at [53].

adapter_context.notes: The actor acknowledged the scope mismatch and applied C003 anyway. A later deck adds C022, specific to this question family, which warns about the 1946_05 shifted year labels. That is a post-hoc, question-shaped card.

remedies.intervention: Cross-printing consistency on each extracted (row label, column): compare the chosen printing with earlier printings of the same label. If the whole row differs from every earlier printing and matches another year's row elsewhere, flag an OCR year-label shift and block the commit.
remedies.why: The actor already had the file list [29] and saw the matching FY1940 row [51]. An automatic diff makes the mislabel explicit instead of leaving it to judgment.

remedies.intervention: Card-scope gate: allow a card only when the task matches its 'applies when' keywords, and require the actor to state the match before using it.
remedies.why: C003's keywords (cagr, total outlays, arc elasticity) do not match this question; [36] notes the mismatch and applies it anyway.

remedies.intervention: Series-location index learned across questions (which issues print which fiscal-year rows of a table, and known OCR label faults per issue), retrieved by table and year.
remedies.why: The mislabel in 1946_05 is a stable corpus fact that Opus found by scanning. An index would hand it to the weaker actor without that scan.

remedies.intervention: Add a 'Not when' to latest-printing rules: not when the latest printing's row disagrees with all earlier printings; verify the year label against a neighbouring row or vintage first.
remedies.why: The actor followed card text literally here, so a scoped rule would likely be followed too. But the root problem is out-of-scope application, which text alone did not prevent.

right_arms_note: No arm was right. All three found the Table 3 'Analysis of General Expenditures' family through the footnote. The prompt arm reached Opus's exact cells and difference at [36] and then abandoned them for a synthesized rebased value. The none arm misread both cells by one column. The cards arm read FY1946 correctly but took an OCR-mislabelled '1934' row from the latest printing.
text_vs_mechanism: Mechanism. The three failures (positional misreads, synthesizing an unpublished input, a card applied out of scope) would all be caught by a provenance plus cross-printing CHECK on the two endpoint cells. The prompt arm had relevant text (L-commit-once, latest-vintage conventions) and not only failed to follow it; the latest-revision emphasis plausibly fed its over-correction.
notes: Each arm failed in a different way on a question where the right table was easy to find, so the difficulty is in cell and vintage hygiene, not search. Both learners later added question-specific rules (C022; L-public-works-column-pwa-housing) with the exact source lines: answer-shaped memory that helps only on a repeat of this question. The generalizable lessons are provenance-only inputs and cross-printing agreement. Opus's per-vintage scan script (scan_pw.py) is a good model for a harness TOOL that lists every printing of a (row, column).
